utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Robinson cannot be with us today due to an urgent matter, so Judge Bonomy and myself will be sitting today pursuant to 15 bis. There's one matter of housekeeping before we go on, which arises out of yesterday's hearing in relation to the exhibits. Judge Robinson noted that a bunch of Prosecution exhibits which had been used during the cross-examination of Mr. Delic would be admitted, but there was some confusion and some certain modification is necessary. So we'll deal with it at the end of Mr. Delic's evidence, together with some remaining Defence items.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, continue your examination, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Janicevic, do you have any direct knowledge about what you only mentioned yesterday in response to the previous question about mass demonstrations of Albanian separatists in Kosovo in 1981?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start answering again. His microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, could you repeat your answer again. Could you start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes, of course. I personally took part in breaking up the hostile demonstrations in 1981. Those demonstrations started on the 11th of March. Their motto was to resolve the social welfare problems of the students, and they went on all the way up to the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacity did you take part in this?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a policeman of the provincial SUP at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of these demonstrations, and what were the messages of the demonstrators? You mentioned a few moments ago that purportedly that was due to the dissatisfaction of the students due to some problems that they were having.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of these demonstrations was extremely nationalist and separatist. They were cheering for Albania and Enver Hoxha. Their slogans were: We are Albanians and not Yugoslavs. Furthermore, their slogans included the following: We are the children of Skenderbeg and the army of Enver Hoxha. From the 3rd to the 4th of April, these demonstrations turned into an armed rebellion, because in addition to the methods they used so far that could jeopardise people's health, they resorted to firearms as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milosevic. Can I ask, Mr. Janicevic, whether you are reading from something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. These are just my preparations from the hotel. I'm just -- I'm not reading this, I'm just sort of glancing at it. Would you like to see this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need that in answering the questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I need it by way of a reminder, to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you prepared it at your hotel room yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been a long time. Yes, last night in my hotel room. If you like to, you can check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please go on. You could have clarified that kind of thing in advance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to the witness rather briefly about all the subjects that I wish to ask him about. I assume that, bearing in mind these subjects, the witness sort of jotted down what I wanted to ask him. If it bothers you if he looks into his notes, the ones that he wrote in his hotel room, as he said, he doesn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few moments ago you said that the demonstrators, since these demonstrations were violent, as you said, even resorted to firearms. Were there any casualties in these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to the best of your recollection and to the best of your knowledge, what was the outcome?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were nine victims. Eight demonstrators and one policeman were killed. Ibrahim Abazi, an ethnic Albanian, was the policeman who got killed. He worked for the provincial SUP. Further on, there were 205 wounded persons, out of which 130 were policemen. The rest were participants in the demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it seems that there were twice as many injured policemen when compared to the demonstrators.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now: In view of your professional work, what was the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija after these demonstrations, from 1981 onwards, throughout that decade, from 1981 until 1990?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1981 until 1989, the political and security situation in Kosovo and Metohija was very complex and difficult. It was complex and difficult because pressures exerted by Albanian separatists and nationalists against Serbs and all other non-Albanians were on the rise and were even more pronounced than before. May I just mention that in this period, from 1981 until 1988, 28.000 Serbs were practically expelled from Kosovo. Serbs only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give some examples of the crimes that you referred to just now, those that happened after these demonstrations in 1981?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many examples, but I'm just going to mention two. The first example is the murder of Danilo Milincic, in the village of Samodreza, near Vucitrn, on the 2nd of June, 1981. And the second example is the murder of Miodrag Saric on the 3rd of July, 1982, in the village of Mece near Djakovica. These are the most impressive examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, can you tell me how you managed to remember these dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the book -- well, I was a policeman and I retired as a policeman only six or seven months ago, or rather, eight months ago, on the 31st of December, 2004. Every day we received bulletins and reports about what was going on in the territory of the province. These are the most impressive examples, and any citizen could remember these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you have a personal recollection of these dates, have you? You didn't need to check anything, you have a personal recollection of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I checked these dates, but I know that it was in 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell me you had checked them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said: I did not recall the exact date, but I knew the year. Is it that important that I've checked the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you didn't say you didn't remember the exact date; you said the exact opposite of that. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do we need to dwell on these events in 1980s? Please move on. Bear that in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. But, as you've heard, Mr. Janicevic was a policeman and a public official for a while. He was president of a municipality. So his testimony can be quite authentic in terms of what happened and how the situation developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, since you spent your entire career as a policeman in Kosovo and Metohija, do you have any other information about crimes, about the form they took, perhaps about some statistics of everything that happened to the detriment of Serbs, Montenegrins, and other non-Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just give a few examples. For example, in the period from 1982 until 1984, ten rapes were committed, and there were 11 attempted rapes of Serb women by Albanian men. There were 286 crimes against Serbs and 1.249 misdemeanours where Serbs were the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think we need ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- answer to the question whether he's done this from memory or from a record. He obviously has referred to a record, and to pick up the point that was concerning His Honour Judge Bonomy, if records are going to be relied upon or to have been relied upon, they should have been made available to us so that I can deal with their authenticity and accuracy. As it is, I shall be cross-examining somebody who has turned to records not available to me, or they may now be coming available. A briefcase is being opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Setting aside the value, he can speak from his personal memory, can't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He can of course speak from his memory if it's relevant, but here we've seen a fairly -- a very precise listing of numbers, and it obviously comes from a record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the source of these statistics, Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source of these statistics that we've referred to is a publication called "Kosovo, the Past and Present." It was published in 1989 by Medjunarodna Politika, a publishing house in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can I take it that you've used the book, written notes out on a piece of paper, and now you're reading from a piece of paper to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not everything, just the figures. I cannot recall the exact figures after 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, by now you should know how to lead a witness. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I personally would like to move to something relevant to this trial about which this witness has personal knowledge. Can we not get up to date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, what you've just been saying, without entering into precise figures because you didn't count all this, but do you have any personal knowledge yourself dating back to those days about the things which you're testifying here; that is to say, the rapes, the killings, the destruction, the destruction done to cemeteries, and everything else that you mentioned? Is that based on your own knowledge or did you learn it from books you've read?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's on the basis of my own personal knowledge. I have spent 33 years working in the Ministry of the Interior, mostly in the police force and involved in public security, law and order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Janicevic. Now, for your testimony here, it's not vital that we quote precise figures. What is more important is to describe what went on, the kind of things that happened. So we don't need to hear exact numbers, figures. So you can limit yourself to your own personal knowledge and experience about the matters in hand here. In tab number 2, we have a brief contribution, a video, which testifies to what you said a moment ago. So may we show that footage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There should really be translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we pause there a minute. Stop the video. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There should be a transcript or translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's not actually audible. Can you deal with it at this moment, with this? Do we need to view more?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you were able to see on the video is the date. There was a "2" at the end. Was it '82, 1982? May we see the video again? And you can also see a Serbian Orthodox cemetery which has been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is a very leading question. Ask questions to the witness instead of you saying everything in advance. Mr. Milosevic, how long are you going to plan to have this witness? You said ten hours?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only for your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we not move on to 1990s right now? And you can deal with the 1980s, if necessary, at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it is necessary, because this is a very important witness. However, if you insist that we move on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the point you're trying to make about the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point that I'm trying to make is the continuation of violence against Serbs, Mr. Bonomy, which is ongoing today as well, with the help of those people of yours who issue orders, and your own state, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Entirely domestic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those remarks -- my microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm satisfied that there is no legitimate forensic purpose for this, in light of the remarks made to support the leading of this evidence, and I, for one, am certainly opposed to any further evidence about the 1980s. We've heard plenty of the historical background already, and we don't need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us hear the evidence in relation to 1990s, in particular 1999, and let's deal with it later, 1980s. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I shall go back to these questions, or perhaps I can just go through them now with respect to the exhibits that have been provided here for you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. So let's move on and look at the most important points in the testimony of Mr. Janicevic, and then later on I'll go back and pick up the questions that I consider need to be asked in the examination-in-chief, and there are a series of exhibits here related to those matters. So just let me consult my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, in preparing for this testimony, we discussed the activities of the KLA and your knowledge thereof and the formation and establishment of that so-called Nerodimska zone, or area, and the KLA brigade which was within its composition. Tell us when and where you arrived at information about the Nerodimlje zone and the brigade, the terrorist KLA brigade, which was within its composition.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd first of all like to say when we first learnt about the formation of some terrorist group, or rather, one terrorist group in the SUP Urosevac area. At the end of 1997, that was, when there was a terrorist attack against a police point in Grlica and the killing of a member, of an Albanian named Dugoli, on the 28th of November 1997. That was performed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by a terrorist group which had been established by Shukri Buja and it was active in the area of Lipljani up to the gorge of Crnojevska. In January 1998, the first staff was established, the terrorist KLA staff, in the Urosevac area, in Jezerce to be exact. However, even before that, there were intimations, or rather, attempts to establish a paramilitary staff which at that time was not called the KLA staff. It was called the paramilitary staff for the defence of Nerodimlje, and this Nerodimlje zone and joining up all the terrorist organisations active in the Urosevac area took place somewhat later on, in the second half of 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, Mr. Janicevic: In tab 10, take a look at tab 10 in the documents you have there - and I think we all have those documents before us - whether they are indeed documents about the Nerodimlje operative zone. And tell us what those documents contain and whose documents they are, their origin and the time they date back to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a translation of this? I'm afraid not. There's no translation. If we could put the tab 10 on the ELMO so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Put the documents in their order on the ELMO, please. They are mostly diagrams, schematics, and I think it will be easy to follow them. Just briefly, let's go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is an RDB, first of all, Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] RDB is the sector for state security of the Republic of Serbia, which came under the Ministry of the Interior at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document of the state security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what date is it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document of the state security dates back to 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, please, what this first diagram is all about, the one we can see there.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the operative zone of Nerodimlje, with the brigades and staffs. The commander of the so-called operative zone of Nerodimlje was Shukri Buja, and his nickname was Sokol, or falcon. He was called Gazetar previously but came to be known as Sokol. And the deputy commander was Ymer Gazi, and his nickname was Fehmi. Then we have Zoran Filmi [phoen]; Cari Lutara [phoen], called Kuri; Xhemajl Xhemajl [phoen], nicknamed Hadzija; Emir Acica [phoen], nicknamed Petrik; Sadiku Ismet, who was the first, in 1996, to set up a sort of paramilitary staff. Then there was Vica Saban [phoen], nicknamed Mudzahedin; Samir Hajrudin, nicknamed Selma, Jashari Milajm [phoen], nicknamed Professor; Fehmi Hajrunahu [phoen], nicknamed Fehma; and a man named Kospat or rather, his nickname was Spat, but we weren't sure of his real name. Now, within the composition of the Nerodimlje Operative Zone, we have the brigade names: The 161st, Ahmed Medziku [phoen] was named later on, after January 1999. And the commander of this brigade was Ramusilje Imi [phoen], nicknamed Granite. Then we have the 162nd Brigade of Agim Bajrami, and it received its name, took the name of the deputy commander who lost his life in fighting the Serb security forces in August 1998. The commander was Iljas Djamil [phoen], and he died fighting the security forces and was replaced by Commander Zarko Cabil [phoen], nicknamed Cori [phoen]. Then we have the 163rd Brigade, or rather, there was the 163rd Brigade with Commander Eli Ziriza [phoen], and it was just a brigade on paper. Ahmed Kaciko [phoen] was the commander who died fighting against the Serbian police, but the commander later on was Eli Riza [phoen], as I said, and he was a former policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, I don't think you have to read all the documents in that detail. But how can we recognise that this document is a RDB document which dates back up to 1999, without any stamps or without any date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document which was compiled on the basis of gathered information during 1998 and 1999. They are operation reports and work in the field, on that basis. I have a piece of paper here which I received, so compiled by the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In preparing for this trial, the lawyers gave me this piece of paper to show to the Trial Chamber, to show that the documents here are original, and this was issued from the state security on the 22nd of June, 2005. So this is just a diagram. In the documents of the operative zone of Nerodimlje, and there are quite a few of those - I think several tabs here, in fact, deal with that matter - have the dates on them, the dates of the documents, when they were compiled and on the basis of what information. But this testifies to their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That kind of letter should have been included in this exhibit and translated. Does this letter say that this document, this very RDB document, is included in that bunch of documents offered by the state security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to have this letter translated and exhibited. Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. It's obviously a document we should see. I don't know if it's been provided to us in any other way. I don't know if the material contained or said to be identified in this letter is material that's been subject to requests by us or by other teams. It's a totally unsatisfactory way of dealing with evidence, because basically, as yesterday with another witness in another section, this witness is trying to produce material that is basically produced by other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm obviously behind everyone here, because I've forgotten what the witness has told us was his connection with the State Security Service. Mr. Janicevic, can you tell me your link with the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The RDB was in a ministry until a few years ago, until 2001. Therefore, the links were firm, close. All the information that the public security received, all their operative reports and everything with respect to the actions of terrorist groups in the area, that is to say, in the area of my own secretariat, were sent in to the State Security Service, which then, on the basis of that information and those facts, compiled reports and made their estimates of the security situation on the basis of that material. They issued collective reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but how do you happen to have the reports, or the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please let the witness answer my question. How do you happen to have the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Belgrade, while I was being proofed, the lawyer gave them to me, the lawyer who proofed me. He gave me copies of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, I don't see any link between you and these documents. But perhaps it can now be clarified by questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who were the lawyers that gave you these documents? You mean associates of the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is not you but they who got these documents from the security service? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it was they. They were provided at their application, at their request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this letter was addressed to those lawyers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think now I understand. Mr. Milosevic, if you clarify this matter further, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just had a brief look while it was on the overhead projector. I saw that the letter was addressed to Mr. Raicevic, who is one of my associates in Belgrade, just as Ognjanovic, Tomanovic, and Rakic are my associates who regularly come here. They filed an application, as they are entitled to, for RDB documents to be provided to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the first thing you have to do when producing a document is to lay foundation of it; how you got possession of it and how can you prove the authenticity of that document, et cetera. So you should have laid that foundation first of all. Let us go on. Just a second. Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the link between this witness and the document that really matters, and we don't seem to have that at the moment. How is it that he in his professional life would come across this document? That's what we need -- at least, it's what I need to know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just took the words out of my mouth, Mr. Bonomy. I was about to say that when I was interrupted. Mr. Janicevic was chief of the Secretariat of the Interior, that means the highest place, leader of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... from you, I want to hear it from the witness, and I don't want to hear it from the witness through leading questions. I want a genuine, spontaneous response from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, you already got that answer at the very beginning, when this witness was talking about his career record. And this is one of the things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Get on with asking the questions, bearing in mind that I obviously have not, probably through my weakness, made the necessary link. Please make it for me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, did you used to be chief of the Secretariat of the Interior for Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which period were you chief of Urosevac SUP?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 June 1995 to 15 April 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this information relate to your territory, the area of responsibility of your Secretariat of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have I established the link sufficiently, Mr. Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. You've shown no basis for his using these documents during his professional life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, when did you see this document first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was common practice while I was chief of the Secretariat of the Interior to have daily briefings involving chiefs of sections and chiefs of SUP. We had a representative of the state security sector in our area, and we exchanged information that was collected on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. My question was: Is it when you were proofed that you had seen this document for the first time, or did you see this document in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this form, I saw the document for the first time during proofing, but I know about 99.99 per cent of the contents from the time when I worked in the area earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... relevant. He could have given evidence without the aid of a document and we needn't be burdened by a document the providence of which is entirely uncertain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And all it becomes is a form of leading question, because this is material produced by someone else that the witness is just reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can we move on to matters which the witness can deal with with his personal experience.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, but I assert that this is also something that the witness can talk about from his personal experience, because without any leading questions on my part, the witness explained a couple of minutes ago that he personally, and his subordinates in the SUP of Urosevac, collected information on the ground, passed it on to the State Security Service, and the State Security Service exchanged information with them. And this document is one of many documents, one of many reports, compiled by the State Security Service based on the information provided by his organs. I don't see what's unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last bit is the bit we don't know. He's only seeing this for the first time because he's involved in these proceedings. There's nothing about this document to indicate that it's official.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that was provided from the archives of the State Security Service at the request of my associates, or rather, the institution that is named -- that has been renamed Documentation and Information Agency. So this document in this form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it, this document? Is it somewhere in this -- is it described somewhere in the letter? It's not in English, so I can't read it and make any -- I can't understand it as it is, and there's nothing on it to indicate it's official, and I don't know if there's something in this letter that tells us with some authority what it was and how it was compiled and in what circumstances. Now, if that's all there, then please bring it out. And if not, let's move on to something that you can authenticate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I asked for, for the letter to be given to me to have a look, because I don't have the letter at this moment before me. The witness has it. I only saw it on the overhead projector. I didn't have time to deal with these technicalities with the witness. Can I get the letter to see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Hand it over to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is from the Council of Ministers of Serbia and Montenegro, National Council for Cooperation with the ICTY. So my associates went through the regular channels they had to go through, this council, and it is addressed to attorney-at-law Moma Raicevic, who is a member of my team, and it says: "Please find enclosed the documentation requested on the 24th of May, 2005. This documentation relates to the activities of the KLA, its crimes and its activities in the Nerodimlje zone. We herewith enclose 65 statements, collected materials of studies, documentation related to murders," and so on and so forth, structure of the KLA, manuals, written orders, et cetera. All this documentation is listed. All of it is signed by the secretary of the National Council -- of the Ministerial Council, rather, through which my associates had to make this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what does it say this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a document that says: "We herewith provide documents related to the Nerodimlje zone." That means all the documents available to them related to the KLA activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's obvious you don't know what this document is, so let's move on to something sensible that the witness can actually speak about and authenticate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may put questions very briefly in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relation to this document. We'll mark the very tab for identification, pending the authenticity is proved. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I just wish to add that, according to my information, Mr. Nice has all these documents in his possession, because before anything was given to my associates, everything was provided to Mr. Nice's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not an issue. Please get on with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably not correct. And it's not the first time that these observations get made and I have to devote some resources to see whether they're accurate or not and it leads nowhere. We may have been provided with this material elsewhere, I simply don't know, but it doesn't seem to be helpful to raise it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you have shown us the first page where we see this diagram. In 1998, when this Nerodimlje zone, and in 1999, when this Nerodimlje zone was established, did you know about this data or did you just find out from the lawyer who provided you with this document?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew about every brigade, about every staff, before they were actually established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not go into all of these details. Turn to page 6, or 7 maybe, titled "Village Staffs."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this? What does it say? Village Staffs attached to the 161st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us disregard all the other staffs. What is written in the middle column, number 3?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Staff of Racak village, commander Bilali Afet, nicknamed Qofa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it says: "Racak, commander, Afet Bilali Qofa, also known as Qofa. Is Rance also listed?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Village of Rance is also there

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, could you indicate the part with your pointer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 3. This isn't numbered, but it's in the middle column. Number 3 is village Racak staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: Which of these villages are in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rance, three kilometres to the west of Racak. Laniste, four kilometres south-west of Racak. Zborce, two kilometres to the north of Racak. Crnoljevo, a kilometre and a half from Racak. Karacica is a bit further away, about five kilometres from Racak. Petrovo and Krajmirovce, seven and a half kilometres. Manastirce, seven to eight kilometres away. Malopoljce, three kilometres away. Burnik is a bit further away. Jezerce is eight kilometres from Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this 161st Brigade covers Racak and the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. The headquarters of the staff of the 161st Brigade was in Rance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A kilometre and a half or two away from Racak?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. All these sub-staffs, as they were called, or village staffs, were linked to the command of the 161st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was tab 10. We won't deal with it any more. Turn to 10.1. What does it depict? What do we see under tab 10.1? It is a series of photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points, please, if I may. If we look back to the sometimes it may be thought artful method of questioning by the accused, we see that he says at line 14 on page 21, Have you seen this? What does it say? Village staffs attached to ... The answer is Correct. And then we've gone through the chart, it being quite unclear to me whether the witness is giving any evidence himself now of these matters or if he's simply reading the chart out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's reading the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is he confirms the content of it. We can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to be difficult, but I reviewed -- incidentally, I reviewed the first four pages of yesterday's evidence overnight and it was striking to me again how easily we are -- not we are allowing, but how easily the accused gets away with effect leading questions time and again because we just can't be resisting them on every occasion. But the rule against leading questions does have a value and it has value because you the Court need to know what is the evidential status of the answers being given. And at the moment it's clear, for example, on this last passage, that there is uncertainty amongst the professional lawyers and judges in Court as to what is actually happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point about that uncertainty, Mr. Nice, is that it will be held against the questioner. The whole point about the rule against leading questions is that the answers are of little value. And therefore, if evidence is extracted in that way, then it will be weak evidence so far as the questioner is concerned. And I, for one, am just exhausted trying to make the point, because it just never gets taken. And there's a limit to how much you can do to try to persuade someone conducting his own case to try to do it with a modicum of common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's position. I'll try to be conservative in my objections. But on the other hand, I am troubled by what I read or reread of yesterday's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's merit in Mr. Nice's point. Let us move on, bearing that point in your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, that has -- that's pointless, because in lists of documents, Mr. Kwon, I just identified the document that I want the witness to comment upon and to say whether that is correct or incorrect. I read what it says at the top, that these are the village staffs of the 161st Brigade. That is what is written there, in order to identify the document. And then he was the one who was enumerating them, explaining where they are, how far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have made the point very clear. Let us move on with the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Janicevic, what is this photo documentation, these photo files in tab 10.1? What does it represent?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photo documentation in tab 10.1 is part of the on-site investigation conducted on the 28th of September, 1998 in Jezerce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we put these pictures on and I can see what they're like, relevance. What's the relevance of this to this trial? If it's going to be suggested that the KLA did bad things in 1998, it may well be this isn't challenged. But what's the relevance of this material at this trial at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't want to lead, so let's look at these pictures. We don't have to look at the first page, but let's look at the next page. Just put it on the ELMO. You don't want me to lead, I shouldn't put leading questions, so just have a look at the next page. What have you got on that? What are these photographs? Let the witness tell you. Because if you let me put the question, then you're going to say: Ah, did I ask him whether it's a church or a mosque or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness: Were you part of the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not personally, but my staff workers were. My crime technicians and scene-of-crime officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you first see the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediately after the on-site investigation. I cannot remember the exact date, but say two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In my view, these are relevant, and I don't see any objection. In the face of the failure of the Prosecution to concede these events, then the accused is entitled to prove them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, we won't put the first photograph on the overhead projector, but please put the second photograph on. Let me not say anything about what is on the photograph. Then the third one. Put the second one first on the ELMO. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are these photographs? This is a set of four photographs. What is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone please be adjusted. The interpreters cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, could you speak into the microphone, please, when you speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the first photograph, in the upper left-hand corner, is a trench that the terrorists dug at the entrance to Jezerce from the direction of Nerodimlje. On the second photograph, in the lower left-hand corner, there is yet another trench that was dug as an extension of the upper trench, in the direction of Nerodimlje, next to the road. The third photograph, in the upper right-hand corner is a barrier on the road, or rather, it's a hole that was dug and then planks were placed over it. It was supposed to prevent the police from entering the village, because if vehicles tried to get in, they would fall into the hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, what were these trenches used for? And do you have some knowledge of your own from the relevant time what they were used for and what kind of activity was carried out from there?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assaults on police patrols in the area, and possibly for defence from the police that would take measures in order to arrest the terrorist groups that were in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the next page and tell us very briefly, what are the photographs on the next page? Again, there is a set of four photographs.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first photograph in the upper left-hand corner is a bunker. The second one is again an obstacle on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similar to --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to what I showed a few moments ago. In the upper right-hand corner it's the same thing, before it was removed. And the last photograph is a terrorist who was killed in a clash with the security forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can uniforms be seen on the photographs where the killed persons are?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In these photographs, we can see their uniforms too, with insignia of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the next photograph. What is on that photograph? You can see part of a red vehicle here, unless I'm leading when I say that you can see part of a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Lada Niva. Rockets can be seen there for a hand-held rocket launcher. And there are also two hand-grenades and some ammunition of 7.9 millimetres. On the right-hand side is a rifle, Chinese-made. That can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the next photograph, the next page, rather. What can be seen on these photographs?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first photograph, in the upper left-hand corner, you can see equipment that was found at their headquarters, as well as uniforms and caps with KLA insignia. On the left-hand side, in the bottom, is part of the body of a killed terrorist. On the right-hand side is a bunker in the lower left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the next page, please. There are only three photographs there.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a trench on the first photograph, from which the terrorists attacked members of the police and army, and from there they also kidnapped citizens who were moving along that road. In the middle photograph there is a parapet in the rocks. And on the third one is a machine-gun, behind which we can see the parapet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are all of these photographs from the on-site investigation after the terrorist action that was carried out on your territory that you saw immediately after they were made, and does this have to do with the investigation that was carried out?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only part of the photographs that were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the ones that we showed, did you see all of them at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw all of them at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how many brigades were there in the Nerodimlje area?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the so-called operational zone of Nerodimlje had two brigades and one brigade that was being established; 161, 162, and 163 was only on paper, because it didn't function because there weren't enough interested people in the territory of the municipality for which it had been established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tell us where and when you came to this information about the establishment of the Nerodimlje zone and those units that they honour by calling them brigades.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got this information through operative work, through police work on the ground, through friendly connections, through persons who collaborated with us and who were part of the top echelons of these organisations in October 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any information contained in tab 11 which speaks of this Nerodimlje Operative Zone of the KLA, including names? And what do you know about this information? What does it constitute?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 11?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... be an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The same thing can be said in relation to tab 11 as tab 10. You didn't see this document in 1999; instead, you saw this document for the first time only recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Recently I saw the document in this form. However, the information that is contained here, I don't know whether you have a translation, but there's information here about the brigades and then the text reads as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the -- can you help us by telling us what the document actually is and how it was compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know how it was compiled before, but it was probably compiled the same way now too. All operative knowledge, all information that members of the public and State Security Service collect are sent to a single point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you say that this information was in a document, and now it appears in this Court in some other form, in a different document. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This information was sent in its original form to the person who processed all the information and who compiled this document. This has to do with the establishment and functioning of this so-called operational zone of Nerodimlje. So this document was compiled on the basis of several documents that were collected during 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who compiled this document, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The state security sector. Probably Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they're people who work in analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say it sounds to me as if you're speculating about what happened, you don't actually know, because you've never seen a document in this form before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document during my preparations, but over the past 30 years, I saw perhaps 300 such documents, this type of document, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So have you any idea why we're not looking at the ones that you were working with in your professional life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean by saying why you are not looking at something that I had not prepared? I don't understand the question, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were familiar with documents which gave the sort of information which is in this document. This is one you've never seen. And what I'm wondering is why we haven't got the ones that you normally saw in your everyday, professional life. Have you any idea, or is that something you can't help with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents that I saw during my professional career - let me repeat what I said a few moments ago - were all submitted to a higher instance. As far as terrorism is concerned, in this situation, the higher instance is the state security sector, and all relevant information was sent to them, indicating that there were terrorist groups that were active, that they were engaged in criminal activity, et cetera. Everything that had to do with them was sent further on to the state security sector, or a particular department in this case. Then they would send it further up to their top echelons of the state security. And then, on the basis of all the documents that they would obtain from a particular area, they would compile a comprehensive piece of information containing descriptions of everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, prior -- yes, I understand. Prior to being proofed for this case, had you ever seen such a document, one of these comprehensive documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw many such documents, but I saw this particular document too. If I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You saw this one when?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We didn't get the answer to that. You saw this document when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During my preparations for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going around in circles here, and I appreciate -- unproductive circles, but it demonstrates at the moment a lack of understanding on your part of what this document is. If you, in your everyday, professional life, saw comprehensive compilations, compiled within the State Security Service office, what I would like to know is why we're not working from them and why we're working from a document that you never saw in your professional life and you actually don't know how it was compiled. Now, can you answer that question? And if you can't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was compiled on the basis of information that members of the service collected. I repeat: Even my information is contained here, information that I personally compiled. That is contained in this document. And I don't understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you may not understand the rule of evidence. Let's move on, briefly. We'll treat these tabs equally, the same way as we did in relation to tab 10. Move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you said just now that in this document we find information that you personally provided to a superior authority, either to your colleagues in the RDB or elsewhere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said that a moment ago. Now, what information did you have at that time which is contained in this document, what information did you have at your disposal at the time when these events took place?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information of the initial stages of the forming of terrorist groups in the Urosevac area, Likud 2, and this is a summary of the information received, information about the establishment of the 161st Brigade staff and the 167th Brigade staff, their overall activity in the area covered by the secretariat. The way they were financed, for instance, the way they collected money for the purchase of weapons, how they sent out their terrorists to Albania in order to procure weapons, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, to what extent do you have direct information, you yourself, collected by your staff and your collaborators, are contained in this comprehensive report?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, over 80 per cent, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is information from your own area which you amassed in the line of duty, your professional duty?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the source information that was sent out to higher instances, the DB, for example, and other ministries?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source information, original information, was sent out and a copy of that piece of information would stay in the RDB or the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Tell me, please: Where was the staff located? So I'm not asking about this document any more, because, as Mr. Kwon said, we would deal with it in the way he stated, once we establish whether it is an authentic document or not. Tell me: Where was the staff of the 161st Brigade and its headquarters located, and who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff and headquarters of the 161 Brigade of the KLA was in the village of Rance. In the initial stages of its inception that's where it was, and for one month after it had been established, that's where it was. The commander of the staff was Muzilica [phoen], nicknamed Cecica [phoen]. And towards the end of 1998, the headquarters of the staff was moved to the village of Petrovo which is also in the Stimlje municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the municipality of Stimlje. Is it part of the territory of the collection of municipalities covered by the SUP of Urosevac, at whose head you were?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including all the villages, all the villages that you're mentioning now, does it come under your area of responsibility as chief of police for the area?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This terrorist brigade, was it active only in your own area or was it active partially in other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, it was active in Lipljani and Suva Reka, those two areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was its action focussed on?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predominantly in the Stimlje municipality and that general area, or rather, in the area of the Crnoljevska gorge, which is where the main road running from Pristina to Prizren lies, via Stimlje, in 1998. And in 1998, we had almost daily provocations and attacks along this road which was used by military vehicles, police patrols, military transport, civilian cars as well, passenger vehicles, and so on. There were many casualties, a lot of vehicles damaged, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on and be even more specific. Tell us where the sub-staff of this brigade was located in the village of Racak that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sub-staff of the brigade was located in the house belonging to Mustafa Mehmed [phoen], I think that's what the proprietor's name was, in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that staff in the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afet Bilali, nicknamed Qofa,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, Mr. Janicevic -- or rather, take a look at the following tabs, that is to say, tab 12 -- let's take them in their order. Tab 12 first, which is a report compiled by -- who compiled the report? You read it out to avoid me asking leading questions. What does it say at the top? What does it say in the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just take a moment to find the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's tab 12.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The report was compiled --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at what it says in the upper left-hand corner. It says: "Republic of Serbia MUP, Urosevac SUP." The fact that it says Republic of Serbia MUP and Urosevac SUP, is that the SUP that you headed?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a document we've seen already?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why are we going over it again with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the most responsible police official is here, under whose leadership these people collected this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's tab 216 in the Jasovic binder. If we could sort out tab 11 at this stage. Is it going to be MFI'd, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, pending the authenticity is resolved and pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, as head of the Secretariat of the Interior and the number-one man leading these authorised personnel, can you confirm the authenticity of the contents of this report and the legality in which it was compiled?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you do that? Tell me how you do that. Were you there when the report was being compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report was being -- was compiled in November 1998 and I read through it personally and sent it on for further work to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would this kind of report have to be shown you? Did it have to be shown you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the general obligation. Every piece of information, every report, even reports of lesser importance, had to come to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 13, do we have another report by authorised personnel belonging to your SUP, the SUP that you headed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I guess this has been already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this report was compiled in keeping with the rules of service governing your Secretariat of the Interior, or rather, the Ministry of the Interior, and that the information contained therein is exact and true?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I do have to observe the formulation of the last part of that question. It's getting by, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having dealt with this matter already with Mr. Jasovic, I don't think it's necessary, but let us move on. What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, as head of the Secretariat of the Interior -- or to avoid asking you a leading question, let me put it this way: Once you receive a report of this kind, did you undertake any steps to check out the information provided, to attempt to look at another source to check out the information or to check out the information contained on the spot, in the actual location?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that every report was checked and investigated and verified through a number of sources, and each operative, every member of the State Security Service, had his associates and friendly ties and informants as well. For this kind of report to be written and compiled, it had to be checked out according to many sources and many times. And this kind of report was sent on to the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me how you did that, when you got this report. What would you do to check out its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before a report of this kind is compiled, is written out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. Once you've got it, what was it you did, you personally, as the chief, to check out its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to explain the process to you. Before such a report is ever compiled, the operative workers dealing with each subject or problem, if you like, write an official report, a short official note about what they're doing and how far they have come. And then that is verified through a number of sources, through the State Security Service's sources. And then, once they have been verified and checked, this kind of report is compiled, which is sent on to the State Security Service ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me a concrete example. What sort of thing would happen when the original note was written here? What check would you personally carry out? Because it's you that's saying that you carried out the checks to vouch for the accuracy and truthfulness of this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A report compiled in this way was sent out to the State Security Service, the State Security Service department, and then they carried on with their verification of this information. Although, before, it was already checked out and verified before it was compiled in this way, and that was done by higher instances than me; the chief of police or the chief of the crime prevention department. So it had to pass by three or four levels before it reached the head of the SUP. And this is the ultimate stage, which is then sent on up above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me to whom this would go, this -- or the previous -- I don't know now which -- I thought you wanted me to concentrate on the previous, the earlier draft, the first note. Who would it go to to be checked before the report was written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the report was written, it was verified by the commanders of the police stations, the heads of department, and the heads of the administrative departments. And each operative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... before it was ever written. Who would it go to and which police offices before it was written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leading policemen; the chief of the police stations or deputy chiefs of police stations in charge of this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your staff are working in a police station. So which other police stations would this go to before it became a report? How many other police stations would it have gone through to be checked, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you understood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The policemen, policemen, when they go in the field and talk to the operatives, when they come back, they write a report or what is known as an official note. That official note is sent out to the assistant or deputy commander. The deputy commander Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then assesses whether the official note should be sent on or whether it should stay there. If he has information saying that it is accurate, it stays. If not, it is rejected. If it is sent on, it is sent on to the inspectors in charge of the lines of work that check it out further still. And if they confirm its accuracy, then they go on to write this kind of report, which is sent to the chief of the department and then sent up to the chief of SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. So we've now established that this all happens within the one police office, I think. Now, what sort of check would an officer, a more senior officer, make on the note --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt. What sort of check would the next officer up from Mr. Jasovic make before processing the matter further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: Operative work is a very complex job, to gather and amass information. For instance, this piece of information, the officer in charge of that police officer, he has his operative positions on the ground. And for every information that comes in, every paragraph, for example, here Zejn Osmani is mentioned. He goes on the spot in the field to check out whether this man Zejn Osmani is really there, what he does, what he's doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Jasovic's superior, when he gets the note, he will go out to check that this person is actually there; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the superior Jasovic. The SUP, the Ministry of the Interior, there is a line of work according to the crime in the area, whether we're dealing with theft, killings, terrorist acts or whatever the type of crime. There are different categories of crimes, I don't want to have to enumerate them all now. And every piece of information, every official note, goes to the source, to the operative worker there, who checks this piece of information out. In this case, Jasovic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you to take this concrete example and tell me who, after Jasovic compiled his first note, would actually do something to check it out and what he would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jasovic did not compile the first official note. Jasovic worked as an inspector. Jasovic received information from the policeman on the ground, and then he verified and checked out that information. And on the basis of the information he gained and the official note, he would compile, go on to compile this kind of report. This report was then sent on up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying Mr. Jasovic did not obtain the information which is contained in this report. Have I got that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partially correct. He did partially. He checked out the information he received. And on the basis of confirmation of that information, compiled this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would be very grateful if someone at the break will identify where in Mr. Jasovic's evidence he told us that that was the way in which he went about his work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before we break, one question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, Mr. Bonomy mentioned a police station. Tell us: How many police stations were there within the frameworks of your Secretariat of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear you. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say four police stations came under your Secretariat of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, do you have tab 13 in front of you, report by Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After Mr. Jasovic produced this document, there was no further mechanism to check the veracity of this document; am I right? This is the final report on the part of that police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the final -- Jasovic wasn't in the police station. Jasovic worked in the department for crime prevention. He was an inspector there. This report was sent on further to the State Security Service, the RDB, for further processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the answer I like to hear. This is the final report. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simply to respond to the question of His Honour Judge Bonomy shortly before the break. I haven't been able to find a passage of the kind he wondered if we could identify. My recollection is rather to the contrary, and indeed I have found, although I've now temporarily misplaced a passage where he gave an explanation that the Chamber may recall of people either coming voluntarily or being brought to the police station for him to speak to, and the clear implication from his evidence as a whole was that it was all personal contacts from him and others at the police station in an interview setting. He never gave -- to my recollection, he never gave evidence to a contrary effect or to the effect that he was relying on derivative information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you just said that your Secretariat of Interior in Urosevac had four police stations.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of those four police stations -- in fact, was one of them the police station in Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had police stations in Stimlje, Urosevac, Strpce and Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people worked in the Stimlje police station?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 50, together with the senior personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How large a territory is covered by Stimlje police station?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire municipality of Stimlje, about 20 or so villages, including Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did policemen who worked at that police station move around the entire municipality of Stimlje, including all the villages?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until 1998. Until mid-1998, I should say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And afterwards, what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After mid-1998, terrorist actions and activities began. Some villages were held by terrorists and clashes occurred, threats, provocations. It was not safe for the police to enter all the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago Mr. Nice quoted Witness Jasovic as saying that he interviewed people who had been brought to the police station. Who would bring those people to the police station, on what account, and how would they end up being interviewed by Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People would pass through police checkpoints, and some of them would behave suspiciously, some would be suspected to be KLA terrorists, some would be suspected of being wanted for various crimes and offences, and they would be brought in, taken into custody. Not only Jasovic, but all the other officers were involved in the work of elucidating these crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
